entry.title: Editorial review: Add note about bgra8unorm read-only storage textures bring deprecated
entry.content:
Description

Use of the bgra8unorm format for read-only storage textures is deprecated. The specification explicitly disallows this, as this format is intended for write-only access and is not portable. Any browser support for this combination is considered a bug.

Chrome previously allowed this, but it is deprecated from version 140 onwards. See https://developer.chrome.com/blog/new-in-webgpu-140#deprecate_bgra8unorm_read-only_storage_texture_usage.

This PR adds a note to make the deprecation clear. Note that I'm not intending to add a browser compat data point for this change, as:

  • It is expected behavior anyway.
  • We don't really want to encourage people to use it in browsers that wrongly allow it.

Motivation

entry.title: Update forbidden request headers in glossary
entry.content:
Description

The spec says Cookie2 and Set-Cookie are forbidden. Looking at the Chrome source code it also checks for Access-Control-Request-Private-Network, which is added to the list in this draft spec.

You can try it out by opening https://example.com/ and doing

await fetch('https://example.com', {
  headers: {
    'access-control-request-private-network': 'aaaaaaaaaaaaaa',
    'cookie2': 'bbbbbbbbbbbbbb',
    'set-cookie': 'ccccccccccccc',
    'Permissions-Policy': 'this one actually gets sent',
  }
});

and looking in the Network tab.

Additional details

Chrome source code: https://source.chromium.org/chromium/chromium/src/+/main:net/http/http_util.cc;l=324-348;drc=c8dc70b538f1bb0862f1be58237d6e945ee81819

Spec: https://fetch.spec.whatwg.org/#forbidden-request-header

entry.title: Add a federated identity guide
entry.content:
This PR adds a guide to federated identity.

It's not finished yet, but it's definitely ready for some review.

What's done

  • an overview of what it is
  • a moderately close look at the main flow in OpenID Connect
  • a short but sufficient (I think) discussion of the use of third-party cookies in federated identity systems

What's not done:

  • a section on using specific identity providers. I want to say, people adding support for federated identity will always need to choose a provider, and providers will greatly reduce the amount of complexity they need to deal with. I think it is most helpful to name specific providers, such as Google and GitHub and (in a slightly different way I suppose) Auth0 but I don't like the idea of seeming to pick winners or entrench monopolies.
  • a section introducing FedCM. I want especially to talk about:
    • how this fixes third-party cookie issues, greatly simplifies the work the RP needs to do, and promises a better and more consistent UX
    • how it's not cross-browser yet (and thus can't really be recommended yet) but that we're hopeful it will become so.
  • probably something tying it together, which should describe some of the limitations of fed ID (especially, about it excluding people who don't want to or can't sign up with your chosen IdP).

Note that preview images are broken because of mdn/fred#904.

entry.title: docs(HTTP): X-Content-Type-Options — mention impact on document sniffing
entry.content:
What

  • Clarify that X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff also affects document navigations:
    user agents should avoid sniffing and treating content as HTML when the Content-Type is incorrect or missing.
  • Add a short subsection “Effect on HTML document sniffing” with references.

Why

  • The current page focuses on scripts and styles; this update reflects the MIME sniffing algorithm behavior for documents as discussed in WHATWG.

How to verify

  • Run yarn start and preview /en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/X-Content-Type-Options.
  • Confirm the new subsection is rendered and links work.

References

  • WHATWG MIME Sniffing algorithm: https://mimesniff.spec.whatwg.org/#mime-type-sniffing-algorithm
  • Discussion: whatwg/mimesniff#98

Fixes #41745

entry.title: Add new docs for OTP authentication
entry.content:
Description

Adds new documentation describing OTP-based authentication. The article discusses three ways: email, SMS, and TOTP (authenticator apps)

Motivation

Developing a series of guides for implementing authentication covering various techniques, including passwords, one-time passwords, federated identity, and web authentication.

Additional details

  • Overall OTP is presented as a second factor or when confirming user intentions (e.g., payments) and not as a general purpose authentication method.
  • TOTP is presented as the most secure delivery method of one-time passwords.
  • Several flaws with email and SMS-based deliveries are discussed

entry.title: Editorial review: Add doc covering bounce tracking mitigations
entry.content:
Description

Bounce tracking mitigations is a privacy-protecting feature available from Chromium 116 onwards, which also has support in Firefox and Safari in similar forms. It is specified here.

This PR adds a page explaining how it works. This is one of the privacy sandbox features that is fully released and being kept, which I hadn't gotten around to documenting.

Note that is is a browser feature, and not a web platform feature. As a result, it doesn't really have a sensible way to record it in BCD.
